justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a current price around $306–$307 for the underlying asset (likely a major index ETF or similar instrument). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, expecting mean-reverting intraday behavior with minimal directional conviction. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $308, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations. At the one-month horizon, I extended that drift further to $310, essentially applying a small annualized growth rate over roughly 21 trading days while acknowledging that the fundamental trend over medium horizons tends to be positive in calm regimes.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility. For a one-day horizon, typical daily moves of around 0.5–1% translate into a fairly tight band of roughly ±$7. As the horizon extends to one week, uncertainty compounds across five trading days, widening the interval to roughly ±$13. At one month, the interval expands to approximately ±$27, which corresponds to roughly 3–4% on either side — consistent with annualized volatility in the 18–22% range applied over a monthly window. I also factored in some additional uncertainty around macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and earnings season dynamics that tend to add event-driven variance beyond pure statistical volatility.

The most significant tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden shifts in Federal Reserve policy signaling, unexpected geopolitical escalation, or a major credit or liquidity event in financial markets. On the upside, stronger-than-expected economic data, a dovish surprise from the Fed, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could drive prices above the upper bounds. On the downside, a sharp inflation surprise, a significant corporate earnings miss from a systemically important company, or a sudden spike in credit spreads could push prices below the lower bounds.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly normal return distributions with modest fat tails. In practice, financial returns exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a Gaussian model implies. If volatility regimes were to shift — for instance, if the VIX were to spike sharply — realized outcomes could fall well outside even the 90% confidence intervals stated here, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where regime changes have more time to manifest.
